lead: A flip-flop stores one bit by feeding its own output back to its input, so the value stays after the input is removed. This memory separates it from the gates of 5.2. It holds flags and forms registers. Only a few universities teach this inside the introductory electrical and electronics unit. The same cell is also called a latch or a bistable multivibrator. A register is n flip-flops sharing one clock.
prereq: You need: 5.2 for NAND and NOR gates and feedback.

sections.h3: SR latch: feedback stores a bit

blocks.text: A latch is two gates with their outputs fed back. In the NOR version, R means reset and S means set. Q and Q̄ are the two outputs, normally complements.

S=1, R=0: NOR 2 sees S=1, so Q̄=0; NOR 1 then sees R=0 and Q̄=0, so Q=1. Remove S and Q stays 1. R=1, S=0 resets Q to 0. S=R=0 holds the old bit. S=R=1 forces both outputs to 0, so Q and Q̄ stop being complements; when both inputs return to 0 the next state is unpredictable. That state is forbidden.
This level-triggered cell is also called a bistable multivibrator: it has two stable states. The feedback loop is the memory. A clock is not needed for this basic latch.

sections.h3: Clocked SR, D and T flip-flops

blocks.text: A clock tells the memory when to change. In a clocked SR latch, clock C enables two input gates. C=0 blocks S and R, so Q holds. C=1 makes the latch transparent and it follows S and R.
A D flip-flop has data input D. At the active clock edge Q becomes D; between edges Q holds. A T flip-flop has input T. At each active edge Q toggles if T=1 and holds if T=0.

Level triggering acts for the whole high or low time. Edge triggering samples only at 0→1 or 1→0. A transparent latch is level-triggered; a true flip-flop is edge-triggered. The clock edge is the single instant that changes the stored bit. D stands for data; T stands for toggle. The active edge is marked on the clock symbol.
JK removes the forbidden state. J sets, K resets, and J=K=1 toggles.
One-line characteristic table: Q(next) = J·Q̄ + K̄·Q at the active edge. The characteristic table lists hold, reset, set and toggle.

In a level-triggered JK with J=K=1, Q toggles and feeds back while the clock is still high, so it toggles many times in one pulse. This is race-around. The output frequency can exceed the clock frequency, and the final state is uncertain. Edge triggering samples once and avoids it.
A register is n flip-flops sharing one clock, so n bits update together. A 4-bit register uses four D flip-flops. All four see the same clock edge. CPU registers use this; see 5.7.

figure.caption: The two NOR gates feed each other: R drives the gate giving Q, S drives the gate giving Q̄, and the loop holds the bit after an input is removed. Notice the feedback edges.

spec.title: Cross-coupled NOR SR latch
spec.aria: Two NOR gates wired as a loop: R drives NOR 1 whose Q output feeds NOR 2, S drives NOR 2 whose Q̄ output feeds back into NOR 1.

examples.question: A positive edge-triggered JK flip-flop starts with Q = 0. Clock pulses arrive with (J,K) = (1,0), (1,1), (0,1), (1,1). Find Q after each pulse.
steps: Pulse 1: J=1, K=0 sets, so Q=1.
Pulse 3: J=0, K=1 resets, so Q=0.
examples.answer: After four clock edges Q = 1; the sequence is 1, 0, 0, 1.

traps: A latch is level-triggered; an edge-triggered flip-flop samples only at the clock edge. Do not treat the names as synonyms.
S=R=1 is forbidden: both outputs become 0, so Q and Q̄ are not complements and the next state is unpredictable.
A level-triggered JK with J=K=1 can toggle many times in one high clock. That is race-around, not one toggle.
D means data, not toggle. A T flip-flop with T=0 holds; it does not reset.

quiz.q: Which SR input state is forbidden?
Why is S=R=1 forbidden in a NOR SR latch?
quiz.a: Both outputs become 0, so Q and Q̄ are not complements; the next state is unpredictable.
Level acts for the whole high or low time; edge samples only at the transition.

quiz.q: A positive-edge D flip-flop has Q=0. D=1 at the rising edge. Find Q.
quiz.a: At the rising edge Q becomes D, so Q=1.

quiz.q: A positive-edge T flip-flop starts Q=0, with T=1 at three active edges. Give the Q sequence.
Why does a level-triggered JK with J=K=1 not toggle once per clock?
quiz.a: Race-around: feedback causes repeated toggles while the clock is high, so the final state is uncertain.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, flip-flops are storage cells in SRAM and register files. Setup and hold times decide when D must be stable around the clock edge. Metastability happens when that timing is violated. Search next: setup and hold time, metastability, scan flip-flop.
